name: Society Garlic
summary: A tender perennial bulbous herb with garlic-scented foliage and edible flowers. It is botanically distinct from garlic chives and true garlic.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Society Garlic as Tulbaghia violacea in Amaryllidaceae and notes it may be confused with garlic chives, Allium tuberosum. This is a species record, not an Allium cultivar.

growth.short: Clumping bulbous perennial
growth.guidance: The extension profile describes a clumping, arching plant about 1–2 ft tall and wide, used in borders, containers and rock gardens. Those dimensions are NC landscape ranges, not indoor-system dimensions.

cultivation.short: Full sun to partial shade; protect from prolonged cold
cultivation.guidance: NC State reports heat and drought tolerance, with better growth when moisture is available during the growing season; in cooler regions it can be grown as an annual or overwintered in a container. No hydroponic compatibility is established.

propagation.short: Vegetative propagation is the documented practical route
propagation.guidance: The species page lists root cutting; the broader NC State genus profile also describes division. This profile does not infer seed propagation from bulbous growth.

flowering.short: Pink-lilac umbels bloom from early summer into fall
flowering.guidance: NC State reports flowering from early summer to fall, with fragrant lilac-pink umbels on tall stalks. Flowers are edible, but this profile does not infer a need to deadhead or a seed-harvest schedule.

harvestUse.short: Flowers and leaves have a mild garlic flavor
harvestUse.guidance: NC State lists leaves and flowers as edible and describes oniony-to-peppery flowers. Use only correctly identified plant material; this is not a claim that look-alike Allium species are interchangeable.

problems.short: Slugs and snails may damage foliage
problems.guidance: NC State reports no serious insect or disease problems but notes that slugs and snails may damage the foliage. No particular control method is assigned because the source does not prescribe one.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited landscape source does not evaluate hydroponic production.

evidence.note: NC State describes clumping, arching growth.

name: Cuban Oregano
summary: A strongly aromatic, fleshy-leaved tropical perennial in the mint family, not a true oregano (Origanum) species.

identity.guidance: NC State lists Cuban oregano, Indian borage and French thyme among common names for Plectranthus amboinicus; it is not an Origanum oregano.

growth.short: Fleshy herbaceous perennial with semi-woody older stems
growth.guidance: The extension source describes plants about 1–3 ft tall and wide and succulent young stems that become semi-woody with age.

cultivation.short: Warm conditions; shield leaves from intense hot sun
cultivation.guidance: NC State notes growth is concentrated in spring and summer, a preference for hot, relatively dry conditions, and that full sun can burn leaves; the source favors some protection from hot summer sun. No indoor light or hydroponic rule is inferred.

propagation.short: Stem cuttings or division
propagation.guidance: NC State reports easy stem-cutting propagation and spring division. It does not establish a seed-starting protocol for this identity.

harvestUse.short: Aromatic leaves are used as a flavoring
harvestUse.guidance: The source describes fragrant leaves with oregano-like aroma and culinary flavoring use. Common name does not make this plant taxonomically equivalent to true oregano.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected source does not evaluate hydroponic cultivation.

evidence.note: Described as a broad, fleshy-leaved herb; habit values summarize the source description.

spread.reason: Regional landscape dimensions are not an indoor guarantee.

spacing.reason: No indoor spacing recommendation is available.

light.reason: Outdoor exposure guidance does not establish grow-light intensity.

name: Moonflower
summary: A warm-climate twining vine with fragrant white flowers that open at night. This identity is Ipomoea alba, not Datura, which is also sometimes called moonflower.

identity.guidance: NC State distinguishes Ipomoea alba as Moonflower and lists Datura stramonium as a separate plant also called moonflower; this entry is specifically Ipomoea alba.

growth.short: Twining vine with nocturnal flowers
growth.guidance: The NC profile describes a rapidly growing climber that can reach roughly 15 ft in its regional conditions; the exact dimensions depend on climate and support.

cultivation.short: Full sun and a sturdy vertical support
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends well-drained soil in full sun and a fence, arbor or trellis. The source describes warm-season rapid growth; no compact-container or hydroponic suitability is established.

maintenance.short: Train on a sturdy support; bring indoors if overwintering in a container
maintenance.guidance: NC State describes moonflower as a vertical climber requiring a fence, arbor or trellis. To overwinter it, the source recommends growing it in a large container and bringing that container indoors; it does not prescribe routine pruning.

flowering.short: Large fragrant white flowers open at night and close near dawn
flowering.guidance: NC State describes large, trumpet-shaped, fragrant white flowers that open rapidly at night and close near dawn, with flowering from midsummer into fall in its regional account. Night-flying moths visit the blooms; this species is distinct from Datura also called moonflower.

problems.short: NC State reports no significant pest or disease problems
problems.guidance: The cited NC State profile reports no significant insect, disease or other horticultural problems. This does not establish immunity; seed-ingestion toxicity is kept in the separate safety section.

safety.short: Avoid seed ingestion; NC State reports low-severity toxicity
safety.guidance: NC State reports low-severity poison characteristics and warns that large amounts of seed may cause hallucinations. Keep seeds away from children and pets and do not use them as food.

propagation.short: Seed propagation is documented for this climbing species
propagation.guidance: NC State documents seed propagation. The 4–6-week start window and soak-or-scarify options are seed-stage instructions kept in the separate Seed Profile, not repeated as established-plant care.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: A climbing garden vine is not evidence of hydroponic system compatibility.

growthHabits.reason: The source describes a twining/climbing vine, a habit not represented by the current controlled vocabulary; retain the botanical description in the Plant Profile rather than misclassifying it as trailing.

height.reason: Vine length depends on climate and available support.

spread.reason: The source range is regional and support-dependent.

spacing.reason: No container or pod spacing is established.

light.reason: Outdoor full sun is not translated to indoor light requirement.

name: Sweet Woodruff
summary: A fragrant shade-loving perennial groundcover with whorled leaves, spreading by rhizomes and seed. Culinary use is limited and has a documented caution.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Sweet Woodruff as Galium odoratum in Rubiaceae and describes its aromatic foliage and flowers.

growth.short: Low groundcover that spreads by rhizomes and seed
growth.guidance: The source describes plants about 6–12 in tall and spreading up to about 2 ft in its regional landscape context; growth may become aggressive in favorable shade.

cultivation.short: Part to full shade and consistently moist, drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and watering during dry summer periods to prevent dormancy. These are outdoor landscape recommendations.

propagation.short: Seed and division are documented
propagation.guidance: The source lists seed and division and describes spread by rhizomes. It does not provide a reliable seed germination protocol here.

harvestUse.short: Aromatic foliage is used in sachets; flowers are edible
harvestUse.guidance: NC State reports potpourri/sachet use and edible flowers, with a warning that large amounts of flowers may have a blood-thinning effect. This is not a broad dietary recommendation.

flowering.short: Small fragrant white flowers bloom in spring
flowering.guidance: NC State describes small, fragrant, four-petaled white flowers in spring. The source also identifies the flowers as edible; its separate caution about large quantities remains in the harvest/use section.

maintenance.short: Use high mowing only if an outdoor patch needs restraint
maintenance.guidance: NC State says the groundcover can become somewhat aggressive in favorable conditions and may be mowed with the mower set high to maintain it. This is landscape-scale management, not a recommendation for a container or indoor system.

problems.short: May spread aggressively; no significant pest or disease problems reported
problems.guidance: NC State reports no significant insect or disease problems, but notes that Sweet Woodruff can become aggressive under favorable growing conditions. Monitor its rhizomatous spread in the garden; no control treatment is prescribed.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No hydroponic evidence in the cited landscape source.

evidence.note: Rhizomatous low-growing groundcover.

height.reason: Landscape dimensions are not used as indoor-system dimensions.

spread.reason: Spread varies with site and rhizome expansion.

name: Sweet Scabiosa
summary: Sweet scabiosa is grown as an annual in cooler regions and may persist through mild winters. Its long-blooming flowers suit fresh cutting or drying; for direct-sale cut flowers, genus-level guidance places Scabiosa at a half-open stage. Needs good drainage, and tall stems may need support.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Sweet Scabiosa as Scabiosa atropurpurea, an annual ornamental. Pincushion flower is a shared common name and does not make it the same taxon as Lomelosia caucasica.

growth.short: Usually annual in cool climates; may persist in mild-winter sites
growth.guidance: NC State describes Scabiosa atropurpurea as generally grown as an annual in cooler regions, with possible perennial persistence in mild-winter sites. It reports poor performance in high heat and humidity south of USDA Zone 7. This regional note does not establish a universal hardiness boundary.

cultivation.short: Full sun, rich alkaline soil, and reliable drainage
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and rich, alkaline soil high in organic matter with good drainage; the plant does not tolerate wet feet. These are outdoor garden conditions and do not demonstrate hydroponic suitability.

propagation.short: Seed propagation is listed
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed as the propagation strategy but this profile does not assign germination temperature, depth or transplant timing not stated by the source.

harvestUse.guidance: The source describes the flower form and garden value; it does not establish culinary use for this species.

care.short: Deadhead to extend bloom, or retain spent heads for garden interest
care.guidance: NC State says deadheading can prolong the bloom period, while leaving spent blooms may add ornamental interest. Choose based on whether continued flowering or seed-head display is the goal; the source does not specify a pruning schedule.

flowering.short: Blooms from late spring into midsummer, sometimes until first frost
flowering.guidance: The regional NC State profile reports bloom from late spring to midsummer, sometimes continuing to first frost. High temperatures and humidity can reduce performance in warmer regions; this is not a cultivar-specific flowering calendar.

support.short: Long flower stalks may need staking to stay upright
support.guidance: NC State notes that the long stalks may need support or staking. Assess the actual plant and exposure; no universal stake height or spacing is specified.

harvest.short: For direct-sale cut flowers, cut at the half-open stage (genus-level Scabiosa guidance)
harvest.guidance: NC State lists Sweet Scabiosa as a good cut flower and attractive dried-flower material. Oklahoma State Extension's cut-flower table gives Scabiosa spp. a half-open harvest stage for direct sale. This genus-level production cue is not a cultivar-specific performance claim or household vase-life guarantee; neither source establishes a postharvest treatment for this identity.

problems.short: Prevent wet feet; watch for minor aphids/mites and local self-seeding
problems.guidance: NC State identifies poor drainage as a root-rot concern and notes aphids and mites as minor issues. It also reports self-seeding and invasive-weed status in some countries. Check local guidance before allowing seed set; this is not a claim that the species is invasive everywhere.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited ornamental landscape page does not assess hydroponics.

evidence.note: NC State characterizes its habit as clumping/mounding.

spread.reason: Regional garden dimensions are not used for indoor sizing.

spacing.reason: No system spacing is documented.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not an indoor light requirement.

name: Sea Thrift
summary: A compact evergreen perennial of coastal and rocky habitats, suited to well-drained rock gardens and containers rather than wet growing conditions.

identity.guidance: NC State lists Sea Thrift, Sea Pink and Common Thrift for Armeria maritima and notes geographic subspecies within the species.

growth.short: Compact clumping perennial
growth.guidance: The NC profile reports 6 in to 2 ft height and up to about 1 ft spread depending on conditions and forms.

cultivation.short: Full sun with sharply drained, often sandy or rocky soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes a preference for full sun and well-drained sandy or rocky soils, especially in cooler coastal conditions, and notes use in rock gardens, borders and containers. Excessive water can cause root rot; these are outdoor landscape uses, not evidence of hydroponic compatibility.

management.guidance: The RHS says no pruning is required for this species. Its UK garden profile also marks it drought-resistant; that regional rating is not a fixed watering schedule or evidence for a controlled indoor system.

propagation.short: Seed and division are listed
propagation.guidance: The extension profile lists both seed and division but does not provide seed treatment or germination instructions.

problems.short: Wet roots can rot; pest reports vary by region
problems.guidance: NC State notes root rot with excess water and lists aphids, slugs/snails and powdery mildew as possible problems in its regional profile. The RHS describes the species as generally pest- and disease-free in UK gardens; these sources differ in regional framing and breadth, so treat the NC State list as possible monitoring cues, not expected or universal problems.

flowering.short: Pink, white or purple clusters from late spring, sometimes into fall
flowering.guidance: NC State reports clusters of pink, white or purple flowers above grass-like foliage from late spring and sporadically through fall. The species includes geographic subspecies and cultivars, so color and timing can vary by form and site.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Rock-garden suitability is not evidence of hydroponic compatibility.

evidence.note: The NC State entry describes a clumping, rounded habit.

name: Caucasian Pincushion Flower
summary: A cool-climate perennial pincushion flower. The accepted genus used here is Lomelosia; Scabiosa caucasica is a botanical synonym, not the annual Scabiosa atropurpurea identity.

identity.short: Species: Lomelosia caucasica; synonym Scabiosa caucasica
identity.guidance: NC State uses Lomelosia caucasica and explicitly lists Scabiosa caucasica as a former name. It is distinct from the annual Scabiosa atropurpurea.

growth.short: Clumping perennial, about 2 ft tall and wide
growth.guidance: NC State describes a mat-forming or clumping perennial and reports dimensions around 2 ft in its regional landscape context.

cultivation.short: Full sun and light, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: The cited source favors sandy or loamy, neutral-to-slightly alkaline soil and full sun. It describes regional garden cultivation only; no hydroponic or indoor parameter is inferred.

propagation.short: Seed sowing and spring division are documented
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seeds sown in spring or summer and division in spring. The page does not give germination temperature, depth, pretreatment or time-to-emergence, so those seed-stage details remain unspecified.

flowering.short: Long flowering season in cool conditions; blue or white heads
flowering.guidance: NC State describes a long flowering season in cool areas and soft blue or white rounded flower heads. Its continuous lavender-blue bloom from early summer to frost is specifically attributed to cultivar 'Butterfly Blue', not to this unnamed species entry.

care.short: Deadhead to prolong bloom; protect from wet winters and heat
care.guidance: NC State recommends deadheading spent flowers to prolong flowering, cutting stems in autumn after flowering, and protecting the plant from wet winter weather. It also reports poor performance in high heat and humidity; the light dry winter mulch described by the source is regional garden advice.

problems.short: Wet soil and hot, humid conditions are the main cautions
problems.guidance: NC State says wet soil can cause rot and that the plant is intolerant of high heat and humidity; it reports no known insect pests or diseases. These are source-reported cautions, not a guarantee that problems cannot occur.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No hydroponic evidence is provided.

name: Common Rue
summary: Common Rue (Ruta graveolens) is an aromatic, blue-green ornamental subshrub and host plant for swallowtail butterflies. NC State warns that contact can irritate skin and large ingestion can cause serious poisoning; this profile does not recommend culinary use.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Common Rue as Ruta graveolens in Rutaceae and describes it primarily as an ornamental subshrub.

growth.short: Woody perennial subshrub with blue-green foliage
growth.guidance: NC State describes a 2–3 ft tall and wide woody perennial subshrub with aromatic, fern-like blue-green foliage. It is short-lived (about five years in the source's garden context) and can self-seed to replace itself; foliage may be evergreen in warmer-winter areas.

cultivation.short: Sun to partial shade; avoid wet soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun to partial shade and moderately fertile, moist but well-drained soil. Rue tolerates drought and dry, rocky conditions, but wet soil can lead to root rot. The regional source suggests winter mulch in northern zones.

propagation.short: Seed, stem cutting and division are listed
propagation.guidance: The source lists seed, stem cutting and division; no seed-starting parameters are specified here.

problems.short: Wear gloves and avoid unsafe ingestion
problems.guidance: NC State reports no serious insect or disease problems but notes root rot in poorly drained soil. The foliage can cause contact irritation; large ingestion can cause serious poisoning. Wear gloves for handling/pruning and do not infer a safe culinary dose from historical or traditional-use notes.

maintenance.short: Prune old wood in early spring; wear gloves
maintenance.guidance: NC State recommends pruning back to old wood in early spring. Wear long sleeves and gloves when pruning or handling foliage because skin contact can cause irritation. Winter mulch is suggested for northern zones in the cited regional guide.

flowering.short: Yellow flower clusters bloom in summer
flowering.guidance: NC State's narrative places yellow flower clusters above the foliage in mid-to-late summer, and its structured Flower Bloom Time field lists summer. Fall appears in a separate fruit Display/Harvest Time field, not the flower-bloom field; the apparent conflict was a field-mapping error. This remains North Carolina source context, not a universal regional calendar. The page notes pollinator attraction and host value for several swallowtail butterflies.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The source does not evaluate hydroponic production.

evidence.note: NC State describes an erect, mounding woody subshrub.

height.reason: Outdoor species dimensions are given in the Plant Profile; indoor or Garden-system height is not established.

spread.reason: Outdoor species dimensions are given in the Plant Profile; indoor or Garden-system spread is not established.

spacing.reason: No indoor or pod spacing is established.

evidence.note: NC State gives full sun to part shade for outdoor cultivation; this is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Garden Angelica
summary: A tall, cool-climate biennial herb with aromatic foliage, young stems and seeds used in documented culinary contexts. It needs a deep outdoor growing site, dislikes root disturbance, and can cause skin photosensitivity; root-harvest guidance varies by region and production method.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Garden Angelica as Angelica archangelica in Apiaceae and cautions that it can resemble toxic plants; verify identity before use.

growth.short: Biennial or short-lived perennial; flowering usually follows first-year foliage
growth.guidance: NC State describes Angelica archangelica as a robust biennial or short-lived perennial: foliage develops in the first year, with flowering and seed ripening in the biennial cycle. Its profile table gives an outdoor height of 3–6 ft and width of 2–4 ft, while the prose says flowering stems can reach 7 ft; retain this as source-reported garden scale, not a container-size prediction.

cultivation.short: Cool climate, moist well-drained soil and room for a deep taproot
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends consistently moist soil and moderately cool conditions, with part shade or full sun in northern climates. RHS recommends moist but well-drained soil, outdoor spacing of 60–90 cm, and says Angelica is unsuitable for containers because it develops a deep taproot; it also notes that plants dislike root disturbance. Keep those dimensions and placement as garden guidance, not indoor or hydroponic specifications.

propagation.short: Seed and second-year root cuttings are listed
propagation.guidance: The extension source lists seed and root cuttings in the second year; it gives no reliable germination timing or indoor protocol.

harvestUse.short: Tender leaves and stalks; ripe seed; root timing not established
harvestUse.guidance: UNH Extension says leaves and stalks are best used young and tender and seeds are collected in late summer or early fall when ripe. NC State also lists roots as a culinary part but provides no root-harvest timing or technique. Correct identification and careful skin protection remain essential because the plant can resemble toxic Apiaceae and its sap may cause photosensitivity/contact dermatitis.

problems.short: Sap may cause photosensitivity/contact dermatitis; verify identity
problems.guidance: NC State warns about photosensitivity and dermatitis from contact and notes similarity to poisonous Apiaceae. Avoid exposed-skin contact with sap and verify identity before any ingestion.

flowering.short: Large summer umbels appear in the flowering year
flowering.guidance: NC State describes small yellowish-white, sometimes pink, flowers in large terminal umbels during summer, followed by aromatic seed. This is normal second-year development in the biennial cycle, not a problem signal.

harvest.short: Tender leaves/stalks and ripe seed; root timing varies by source and production context
harvest.guidance: UNH Extension says leaves and stalks are best used young and tender and seeds collected when ripe in late summer or early fall. NC State lists roots as culinary but provides no harvest method. For commercial Ontario production, OMAFRA describes a single root harvest in early autumn after the second year and specifies a modified potato harvester; this is regional crop guidance, not a household method. University of Missouri Extension gives conflicting root timing within one publication: its general root section says late fall or early spring, while its Angelica entry says late summer of the second year. Keep those source and production contexts distinct; no universal home root-harvest date or technique is established.

care.short: Cut back after flowering; removing flower heads before seed may extend the plant's life
care.guidance: RHS advises cutting angelica back to the base after flowering. Although Angelica archangelica is usually monocarpic, RHS says it may last another year if flowers are removed just after flowering or before seed set; do not promise this will extend every plant's life.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: RHS advises against container culture because of the deep taproot; this and landscape guidance do not establish performance in or incompatibility with any particular hydroponic system.

evidence.note: NC State describes a robust, erect herb.

height.reason: Outdoor stature is not translated into indoor system size.

spread.reason: No indoor spread evidence.

spacing.reason: No indoor spacing or pod capacity is documented.

light.reason: Outdoor exposure is not indoor grow-light requirement.

name: Blazing Star
summary: A North American perennial with upright flower spikes that open from the top down and provide pollinator habitat. It establishes from seed or corms; leave some dead stems standing for native stem-nesting bees.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Blazing Star/Gayfeather as Liatris spicata and distinguishes it from other species commonly called blazing star.

growth.short: Clumping perennial; published landscape-height ranges differ
growth.guidance: NC State reports 3–6 ft for this species in its regional plant profile; Wisconsin Extension reports 2–5 ft for Liatris spicata. These landscape ranges overlap but differ, and cultivars and conditions affect height, so the profile preserves both rather than choosing a single mature value. Corms and shallow fibrous roots are documented by NC State; landscape dimensions are not indoor dimensions.

cultivation.short: Full sun is preferred; use drained soil that does not stay wet
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun to partial shade and average-to-moist, well-drained soil; Wisconsin Extension says full sun is best, though some shade is tolerated, and warns that overly wet soil can rot plants. Water regularly during the first growing season to establish roots; established Liatris is fairly drought tolerant. These are outdoor garden conditions, not an indoor light tier or hydroponic recipe.

flowering.short: Small flowers open from the spike tip downward
flowering.guidance: Wisconsin Extension reports Liatris spicata flowering from July through September in its regional context and describes the unusual top-to-bottom opening sequence. Bloom timing varies by location; the sequence is a normal development cue, not a cultivar-specific calendar.

care.short: Leave short dead stems standing for native nesting bees
care.guidance: NC State recommends cutting dead stems back to 12–24 in (30–60 cm) and leaving them standing until they disintegrate because native bees nest in hollow stems. Wisconsin Extension advises regular watering during establishment and good drainage through wet winters. This maintenance guidance supports wildlife habitat; it is not a pruning requirement for flowering.

propagation.short: Seed or corm propagation is documented
propagation.guidance: NC State says the species most often propagates by seed and also forms colonies from corms. Exact germination conditions are not specified in this Plant Profile.

harvest.short: For drying, cut spikes when half to two-thirds of the flowers are open
harvest.guidance: Wisconsin Extension recommends harvesting Liatris spikes for drying when roughly one-half to two-thirds of the flowers are open, then hanging them upside down in a protected place to air-dry for about three weeks. This is genus-level guidance for cut/dried flowers, not a promise of household vase life.

harvestUse.short: Pollinator plant and useful cut/dried flower
harvestUse.guidance: The flowers attract bees, butterflies and other insects and are used as fresh or dried cut flowers. Cut-flower harvesting and wildlife stem retention serve different purposes; leave dead stems after the season where appropriate.

problems.short: Support is conditional; saturated winter soil can rot plants
problems.guidance: NC State notes that taller stems may flop and need staking. Wisconsin Extension says spikes generally remain upright and staking is usually unnecessary unless soil is very fertile and moist; assess the actual plant rather than applying a universal support rule. Wisconsin also warns that overly wet soil can cause rot. NC State identifies two Liatris moths whose larvae use this species, so their presence is not by itself evidence of a generalized pest outbreak.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor prairie and garden cultivation do not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: NC State describes a clump-forming perennial with upright spikes.

height.reason: Published landscape ranges differ and are not indoor dimensions.

spread.reason: No indoor spread evidence.

spacing.reason: No container or pod spacing is documented.

light.reason: Outdoor sun exposure is not indoor light intensity.

name: Snow-in-Summer
summary: A silver-foliaged perennial groundcover that forms mats and produces white flowers. It spreads by runners and may self-seed; heat, humidity and poor drainage can limit performance.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Snow-in-summer as Cerastium tomentosum, a perennial native to Italy, and lists several other common names for the same species.

growth.short: Low mat-forming perennial with runners
growth.guidance: The regional source describes a mat around 6 inches high with flower stems rising above it; spread is by underground runners and varies by site.

cultivation.short: Full sun and dry-to-medium, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State notes poor performance in high summer heat/humidity and root rot in poorly drained sites. Spring pruning is preferred; it advises not to prune in fall.

propagation.short: Seed/self-seeding, division and cuttings are listed
propagation.guidance: The plant self-seeds if spent blooms remain and can also be propagated by division or early-summer cuttings. No germination protocol is supplied.

problems.short: Root rot and heat/humidity stress
problems.guidance: NC State lists root rot in poorly drained soil and reduced performance in hot, humid climates; aggressive spread can make it weedy in cooler settings.

flowering.short: White star-shaped flowers rise above the mat in late spring
flowering.guidance: NC State describes white star-shaped flowers in late spring to early summer, on stems rising about 8–12 inches above the low foliage mat. Flowering and spread vary with site and climate.

care.short: Trim in spring, not fall; remove spent blooms to limit self-seeding
care.guidance: NC State advises pruning in spring rather than fall, removing spent blooms if self-seeding is unwanted, and dividing every few years. It also notes that large beds can be mowed on a high setting; avoid treating this spreading groundcover as a compact clump.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Groundcover landscape use does not establish hydroponic compatibility.

evidence.note: The species forms a spreading mat.

height.reason: Outdoor groundcover dimensions are not indoor size evidence.

spread.reason: Site-dependent spread by runners is not fixed.

spacing.reason: No indoor spacing is available.

light.reason: Outdoor full sun is not indoor light intensity.

name: Lamb's Ear
summary: A silver, velvety-leaved perennial groundcover valued for foliage. It spreads by stems rooting at nodes; wet foliage and high humidity can encourage rot.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Lamb's Ear as Stachys byzantina and lists Stachys lanata and S. olympica as former names.

growth.short: Low-spreading perennial foliage clump
growth.guidance: NC State describes a dense clump of thick, woolly silver-green leaves; dimensions and leaf size vary among cultivars, none of which is assigned here.

cultivation.short: Full sun to partial shade; keep foliage dry and roots drained
cultivation.guidance: The source recommends dry-to-medium, well-drained soils and warns that wet leaves and high-humidity summers invite disease. It notes division every 2–4 years in garden conditions.

propagation.short: Division is documented; seed details are not provided
propagation.guidance: NC State identifies division as a practical propagation route. Although it also lists seed, no seed protocol is provided here; the species should not be treated as seed-impossible.

problems.short: Excess moisture can cause leaf rot
problems.guidance: NC State notes susceptibility to leaf rot in high humidity or excessive rain; site drainage and avoiding persistently wet leaves are central to the cited guidance.

flowering.short: Small purplish-pink spikes appear in summer
flowering.guidance: NC State describes small summer flowers on erect spikes. It recommends removing the flower stalks when the foliage is the main ornamental feature, which also helps keep the plant compact; leaf size and habit vary among cultivars.

care.short: Remove flower stalks for a compact foliage display; divide as needed
care.guidance: NC State says spent or developing flower stalks may be removed to emphasize foliage and maintain compact growth, and that division may be needed about every 2–4 years in garden conditions. The plant can spread aggressively where conditions suit it.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The landscape profile does not evaluate hydroponics.

name: Globe Thistle
summary: A clump-forming perennial with spherical blue flowerheads, useful in dry borders and pollinator gardens. Its deep taproot makes division and transplanting difficult.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Blue Hedgehog/Globe Thistle as Echinops ritro and places it in Asteraceae.

growth.short: Clumping perennial with spiny foliage and globe-shaped flowers
growth.guidance: The extension profile reports about 3–4 ft height and 2–2.5 ft spread in landscape conditions and describes a compact clump with blue spherical heads.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained soil; rich shade can cause flopping
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and medium-moist to dry, well-drained soil; partial shade or rich soil may produce lanky stems. Staking may be needed.

propagation.short: Root cuttings/division are listed; seed protocol not supplied
propagation.guidance: The source lists division and root cutting but notes taproot-related difficulty. It does not give a seed-starting protocol in this profile.

harvestUse.guidance: NC State describes showy blue flowerheads and pollinator value. No edible use is established in the cited source.

flowering.short: Blue globes bloom from midsummer into September
flowering.guidance: NC State describes spherical blue flowerheads appearing from midsummer through September. The species-level record does not assign a cultivar-specific color shade or bloom duration beyond the source's regional account.

care.short: Deadhead to encourage rebloom or prevent unwanted self-seeding
care.guidance: NC State says deadheading spent blooms can encourage reblooming and advises cutting before seed set if seedlings are unwanted. For dried arrangements, it recommends cutting flowerheads while young; this is an ornamental harvest cue, not a food use.

problems.short: Watch for wet-soil rot, mildew and occasional pests; stems may flop
problems.guidance: NC State reports no significant insect or disease pests but lists aphids, leaf miners, thrips, slugs and snails to monitor. Overwatering or poor airflow can contribute to root rot or powdery mildew; rich soil or partial shade can produce lanky stems that sometimes need staking.

name: Clary Sage
summary: A fragrant biennial or short-lived perennial sage with ornamental flower bracts and perfumery use. It is distinct from culinary common sage and other Salvia species.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Clary Sage as Salvia sclarea and distinguishes its perfumery/wine uses from other sages. No cultivar is specified.

growth.short: Large biennial or short-lived perennial
growth.guidance: The source reports about 2–5 ft height and 2–3 ft spread in garden conditions; flowering stems carry whorls of fragrant flowers and bracts.

cultivation.short: Full sun, drained soil; avoid wet winter conditions
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes tolerance of dry, gravelly and sandy soils and warns against wet winter soil. Rich, over-fertilized soil can produce tall plants with fewer flowers.

propagation.short: Seed/nutlet propagation is documented
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed (nutlet) propagation for this species. This Plant Profile records the propagation route only; sowing and germination instructions belong in Seed Profile and are not supplied here.

harvestUse.short: Fragrant foliage/flowers have perfumery and flavoring uses
harvestUse.guidance: NC State reports traditional flavoring in wines and liqueurs and perfumery use. This is not a safety or dosage recommendation for essential oil.

flowering.short: Fragrant white-to-pink flowers are reported June–August
flowering.guidance: NC State describes showy, fragrant white, lavender and pink flowers from June to August in its regional garden account. Bloom timing may shift with climate; no cultivar is assigned here.

care.short: Cut fading stalks near the ground to encourage another flush
care.guidance: NC State recommends cutting the stalks back near the ground as flowers fade to encourage a second flush of growth and flowering. It also cautions that rich, heavily fertilized soil can produce taller plants with fewer flowers and that wet winter soil should be avoided.

problems.short: Wet winter soil and excessive fertility can reduce performance
problems.guidance: NC State reports no significant insect, disease or other plant problems in its profile, while specifically warning against wet winter soil and noting fewer flowers in rich, excessively fertilized soil. This is not a claim of universal immunity.

name: Butterfly Weed
summary: A North American native perennial milkweed valued for pollinators. It establishes slowly from seed, develops a deep taproot and is best left undisturbed after establishment.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Butterfly Weed as Asclepias tuberosa, a tuberous-rooted native in Apocynaceae. It is distinct from other milkweed species.

growth.short: Upright perennial in clumps, about 1–3 ft tall
growth.guidance: The cited regional profile describes clumping growth and a deep taproot; it says flowers may take two to three years after seed-grown establishment.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained, often dry-to-medium soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes tolerance of dry, poor soil and cautions against transplanting after the deep taproot develops. Site conditions are outdoor-specific.

propagation.short: Seed grows readily; avoid disturbing established taproots
propagation.guidance: The source says it grows easily from seed and may self-seed; established plants do not transplant well. This does not supply germination pretreatment or timing.

problems.short: Watch for aphids and wet-soil crown rot; host caterpillars are normal
problems.guidance: NC State reports aphids, crown rot in wet poorly drained soil, rust and leaf spot. Monarch and milkweed tussock moth larvae use this species as a host, so their presence is not by itself evidence of a plant-health problem. The clear sap can irritate skin.

flowering.short: Yellow-orange clusters; deadheading can extend bloom
flowering.guidance: NC State describes showy yellow-orange flower clusters and reports May–August flowering in its regional profile. It states that deadheading can ensure more blooms through the season; local timing may differ.

care.short: Remove follicles before they split to limit self-seeding
care.guidance: After bloom, remove developing follicles before they split if you do not want seedlings; leave them to mature if self-seeding is desired. NC State also reports that deadheading can encourage more flowers. Avoid disturbing the established deep taproot.

safety.short: Ingestion can cause illness; clear sap may irritate skin and eyes
safety.guidance: NC State lists low-severity poisoning characteristics if plant parts are eaten in quantity and warns that the clear sap can cause contact dermatitis and eye irritation. Do not treat historical medicinal names or uses as safe-use guidance; wear gloves when handling sap.

name: Wild Bergamot
summary: A North American native perennial herb with aromatic leaves and pollinator-rich flower heads. Drought stress can increase susceptibility to powdery mildew.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Wild Bergamot as Monarda fistulosa and distinguishes it from the more colorful Monarda didyma cultivars often called bee balm.

growth.short: Clumping perennial, commonly 2–4 ft in regional gardens
growth.guidance: The extension profile describes a clumping herb and flower heads blooming through summer; regional varieties can differ in flower color and leaf pubescence.

cultivation.short: Full sun and moderately moist soil; maintain airflow
cultivation.guidance: NC State notes drought tolerance but increased mildew susceptibility under water stress, and identifies crowded, poorly ventilated stands as a mildew risk. It recommends retaining dead stems for nesting bees.

propagation.short: Seed is listed; protocol is not detailed here
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed propagation but does not establish sowing depth, temperature or duration in this profile. Do not substitute a different Monarda species protocol.

harvestUse.short: Aromatic leaves are used in teas
harvestUse.guidance: The source describes aromatic foliage used in teas and showy flowers used by pollinators. This is species-level regional guidance.

problems.short: Powdery mildew and rust can occur
problems.guidance: NC State lists powdery mildew, particularly with crowding or water stress, and rust. It reports relative resistance to mildew for this species but not immunity.

flowering.short: Summer flower color varies among regional varieties
flowering.guidance: NC State describes three varieties in North Carolina that differ in flower color and leaf pubescence. The entry remains an unspecified species-level identity, so no one variety's color or foliage traits are assigned to it.

care.short: Improve airflow; retain shortened hollow stems for nesting bees
care.guidance: NC State recommends pruning stems to increase airflow when mildew is a concern. After the season, cut dead stems to about 12–24 inches and leave them standing until they disintegrate to support stem-nesting native bees; this is habitat management, not a disease treatment.

name: Mexican Sunflower
summary: Tithonia rotundifolia is a tall, branching annual with coarse, hairy foliage and orange-red flowers. NC State reports 3–6 ft height; Wisconsin Extension reports 4–6+ ft, so the regional ranges are kept distinct rather than averaged. Its flowers attract pollinators and can be used as cut flowers; no cultivar is assigned.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Mexican sunflower as Tithonia rotundifolia, an annual native to Mexico and Central America. No named cultivar is assigned.

growth.short: Tall, erect and branching annual; outdoor size varies by source
growth.guidance: NC State reports a regional garden range of 3–6 ft tall and 2–3 ft wide. Wisconsin Extension reports 4–6+ ft tall and describes a branching, somewhat gangly habit. These are regional species-level outdoor observations, not a single reconciled maximum, indoor footprint or promise for a particular cultivar. Wisconsin Extension describes coarse, hairy, ovate-to-triangular leaves, sometimes three-lobed, and brittle stems.

flowering.short: Orange-red flower heads bloom from mid-summer into fall or frost
flowering.guidance: NC State describes flower heads up to about 3 inches across, with orange-red rays and yellow-orange centers, blooming from mid-summer into fall. Wisconsin Extension reports flowering from mid-summer until frost in its regional context. Both describe attraction to bees, butterflies and hummingbirds; the seasonal endpoint depends on site and frost timing.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained, poor-to-average soil; protect tall stems
cultivation.guidance: NC State and Wisconsin Extension recommend full sun and well-drained soil. Wisconsin Extension advises against rich soil or heavy fertilization because excess foliage can produce weak stems; it suggests about 2 ft between plants when neighboring plants provide support, or 3–4 ft for staked plants. These are outdoor garden spacings, not hydroponic pod distances. Shelter from strong wind and stake where needed; drought tolerance does not mean newly established plants should be left dry.

maintenance.short: Pinch or shear early growth; stake and deadhead as needed
maintenance.guidance: Wisconsin Extension says pinching encourages bushier growth and that shearing plants back by about one-third in early summer can promote branching and reduce height somewhat. Both Wisconsin and NC State recommend staking when needed; NC State and Wisconsin advise deadheading spent flowers to prolong bloom. These are conditional garden practices, not a cultivar-specific pruning calendar.

propagation.short: Sow after frost or use transplants
propagation.guidance: NC State says to start from seed after the last frost date or use transplants. This established-plant profile does not repeat a seed-starting protocol; see the Seed Profile for seed-to-seedling details.

problems.short: Brittle stems and fragile flower stalks can bend or break
problems.guidance: Wisconsin Extension describes brittle stems and fragile hollow flower stalks that can bend and are sometimes broken by birds. It reports few pest problems and low deer preference; these observations do not guarantee pest-free plants or diagnose a broken stem's cause.

harvestUse.short: Cut as petals unfurl; handle the delicate neck carefully
harvestUse.guidance: The University of Kentucky Center for Crop Diversification's Tennessee cut-flower profile recommends harvesting Tithonia rotundifolia when petals have unfurled from the center and notes a delicate neck. This is a regional production cue, not a cultivar-specific schedule or vase-life guarantee. NC State and Wisconsin Extension also identify the species as a cut flower and pollinator plant; Wisconsin describes its hollow flower stalks as fragile. No edible use is asserted.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Garden flower recommendations do not establish hydroponic compatibility.

evidence.note: NC State lists an erect habit for the species; Wisconsin describes branching, but the existing compatibility value is limited to the directly supported upright category.

height.reason: Institutional regional sources differ: NC State reports 3–6 ft, while Wisconsin Extension reports 4–6+ ft. No single cultivar or reconciled maximum is represented.

name: Common Yarrow
summary: A widespread perennial wildflower with fern-like foliage and flat flower clusters. It spreads by rhizomes and seed and may become aggressive; named garden cultivars are not represented.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies common yarrow as Achillea millefolium and notes that flower colors vary among garden varieties; this record is the species, not a cultivar.

growth.short: Spreading perennial with fern-like foliage
growth.guidance: The extension profile gives an approximate 1–3 ft landscape range and describes spreading via rhizomes and seed; cultivar habit and color can differ.

cultivation.short: Full sun and well-drained soil; tolerates poor soil and drought
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes yarrow as tolerant of poor soil and drought, with full sun and well-drained soil preferred. Avoid persistently wet soil, which can cause root rot; site and cultivar performance may vary.

propagation.short: Seed, division and rhizomes are documented
propagation.guidance: The source says yarrow spreads by seed and rhizomes and is readily divided. No seed-starting parameters are established here.

harvestUse.short: Fresh stems: cut before excessive pollen shed
harvestUse.guidance: For fresh cut-flower stems, Mississippi State recommends harvesting when most flowers in the cluster are open, before excessive pollen shed; cut during cooler morning hours and hydrate promptly. For drying, harvest fully colored heads before browning. This is farmer-florist guidance, not a home-storage guarantee. NC State describes cut/dried use and pollinator value and advises gloves because contact dermatitis is possible.

problems.short: Spreads aggressively; wet-soil rot and skin irritation are useful cautions
problems.guidance: NC State warns that the species can spread aggressively by rhizomes and seed and reports root rot in overly wet soils; stem rot and powdery mildew are described as rare. It also advises gloves because plant contact can cause dermatitis.

flowering.short: Flat-topped pale flower clusters can continue into fall
flowering.guidance: NC State describes tiny whitish radial and disc flowers in flat-topped clusters from early to mid-summer into fall. Garden varieties can have other colors; this species-level profile does not assign a cultivar color.

care.short: Deadhead to prolong bloom and reduce seed spread
care.guidance: NC State recommends deadheading flowers to prolong blooming and minimize spread by seed. The species also spreads by rhizomes, so deadheading alone does not contain its growth.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Landscape/perennial references do not establish hydroponic suitability.

name: Blue False Indigo
summary: A long-lived North American native perennial with blue pea-like flowers and a deep taproot. It supports pollinators but is difficult to transplant once established.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Blue False Indigo as Baptisia australis in Fabaceae; several Baptisia species and named hybrids exist, but none is assigned here.

growth.short: Clumping perennial with a deep taproot
growth.guidance: NC State reports about 3–4 ft tall and 2–4 ft wide in garden settings; the taproot supports drought tolerance but makes transplanting difficult.

cultivation.short: Full sun to part shade in well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: The source describes average well-drained soils and drought tolerance. Shaded plants may become leggy or droop; these are regional landscape observations.

propagation.short: Seed and stem cuttings are listed
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seeds or stem cuttings, while warning that the deep taproot makes transplanting difficult. Germination conditions are not provided in this record.

harvestUse.short: Ornamental flowers and seed pods; pollinator host
harvestUse.guidance: The source describes blue flowers attractive to insects and seed pods useful as dried ornament. It also reports low-severity toxicity if parts are eaten; do not use as food.

problems.short: Ingestion is unsafe; major pest or disease problems are not reported
problems.guidance: NC State reports low-severity poisoning characteristics if plant parts are eaten in quantity and no major insect or disease problems for this species. Keep it away from children and pets; do not use it as food. The absence of major listed problems is not a guarantee of pest-free growth.

care.short: Prune after flowering only if seed pods are unwanted or shaping is needed
care.guidance: NC State recommends pruning after flowering when seed pods are not desired and for shaping. If the ornamental pods are wanted, leave the stems; the deep taproot makes established plants difficult to move.

name: Flowering Tobacco
summary: A fragrant, night-flowering species grown ornamentally. Its long summer-to-frost display and tall form suit outdoor borders and nighttime gardens; it is often confused with compact Nicotiana hybrids that differ in height and flower-opening behavior.

metrics.note: NC State species account; regional garden range

metrics.note: NC State recommendation for outdoor planting; not pod spacing

identity.guidance: NC State distinguishes true N. alata from compact nursery hybrids such as Nicotiana × sanderi; this species record does not include those hybrids.

growth.short: Tall annual or tender perennial; dimensions are regional garden context
growth.guidance: NC State gives a 3–5 ft height and 1–2 ft width for its species account. These are regional outdoor garden dimensions, not a guaranteed size for every climate or an indoor-system specification. True N. alata is taller than some compact nursery hybrids; no hybrid dimensions are assigned to this species identity.

cultivation.short: Full sun to partial shade; keep soil moist but well drained
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun to partial shade and moist, well-drained soil with abundant organic matter. The species has low drought tolerance; afternoon shade may help in hot southern climates. Its 12–14 in planting spacing is an outdoor garden recommendation, not indoor pod spacing. NC State also cautions against placing it near tomato, potato or pepper crops because nightshades can share viruses.

flowering.short: Tubular, fragrant flowers open at night from summer into frost
flowering.guidance: NC State describes true N. alata as bearing showy tubular flowers that open for one night, with a long bloom season from early summer to the first frost; fragrant flowers attract night-flying moths. Flower colors vary. Compact nursery hybrids such as N. × sanderi may be shorter, unscented and open by day; those hybrid traits are not transferred to this species record.

propagation.short: Seed propagation is documented; distinguish the species from compact hybrids
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed propagation for true Nicotiana alata and notes the seeds are extremely small. It supplies no numeric germination protocol; compact-hybrid traits are not transferred to this species entry.

problems.short: Keep ornamental tobacco separate from edible crops
problems.guidance: The source warns about shared tobacco mosaic virus risk with other nightshade crops. Treat as an ornamental identity; no food use is stated.

name: Common Snapdragon
summary: Common snapdragon is grown as a short-lived annual with tall and dwarf selections. Manage its cut-flower stems by bloom stage, stake tall forms when needed, and keep species-level edible-flower guidance separate from cultivar claims.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Common Snapdragon as Antirrhinum majus in Plantaginaceae. Several tall and shorter cultivars exist, but this identity does not represent a particular cultivar or color series.

growth.short: Erect to straggling flowering herb
growth.guidance: NC State describes a short-lived tender perennial treated as an annual in cultivation, with both tall and shorter cultivars. Its broad species-level dimensions are not attributed to any one cultivar.

cultivation.short: Full sun to partial shade; avoid overhead watering
cultivation.guidance: The source recommends moist, rich, well-drained soil in full to partial sun, advises avoiding overhead watering, and notes that plants can languish in summer heat. Tall forms may need staking; no hydroponic method is established.

harvestUse.short: Cut flowers; blossoms are edible but bitter
harvestUse.guidance: NC State lists snapdragons as useful cut flowers and says the edible flowers are bitter and best used as garnish. This is species-level guidance, not a recommendation to eat unidentified ornamental flowers.

problems.short: Rust and fungal diseases are notable concerns
problems.guidance: NC State reports significant susceptibility to rust and also lists molds, fungal leaf spots, downy mildew, wilt and root rots. These are reported risks, not a claim that every plant will develop them.

care.short: Maintain moisture and avoid overhead watering
care.guidance: NC State notes low drought tolerance and advises avoiding overhead watering. Keep the root zone from drying severely while avoiding prolonged saturation; the source does not give a fixed irrigation interval. This is species-level garden guidance.

flowering.short: Bloom runs from early summer to fall; colors depend on cultivar
flowering.guidance: NC State reports flowering from early summer through fall and many color combinations across cultivars. This unnamed species profile does not promise a particular color, flowering duration, or heat performance for a seed packet.

support.short: Tall cultivars may need staking; dwarf selections are different
support.guidance: NC State says tall snapdragon plants may need staking. Because this identity includes no selected cultivar, assess actual stem height and exposure rather than applying the advice automatically to dwarf forms.

harvest.short: For cut stems, harvest when the lower third to half of the spike is open
harvest.guidance: Mississippi State Extension's farmer-florist guide recommends harvesting snapdragon stems when florets on the lower third to half of the spike are open. This is species-level cut-flower production guidance; exact handling and vase life vary by cultivar and production conditions and are not assigned here.

name: Pink Turtlehead
summary: A clumping native perennial associated with moist woods, swamps and bogs. It is useful for moist garden settings, not evidence for a water-culture system.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Pink Turtlehead as Chelone obliqua in Plantaginaceae and notes its southeastern/central North American range.

growth.short: Clumping perennial, around 2–3 ft tall
growth.guidance: The regional profile describes clumps about 2–3 ft tall and 1–2 ft wide in moist outdoor settings.

cultivation.short: Partial shade to dappled sun with moist, fertile soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes moist-to-wet habitat and adaptable fertile garden soil from sun to shade. This does not imply hydroponic suitability or standing-water cultivation in containers.

propagation.short: Seed, division and cuttings are documented routes
propagation.guidance: NC State lists propagation by seed, division or cuttings. The selected profile does not provide a sowing schedule, germination temperature or establishment protocol; those details are not inferred here.

flowering.short: Pink-to-purple spikes bloom from late summer into fall
flowering.guidance: NC State describes snapdragon-like rose-to-purple flowers in terminal spike-like clusters from late summer to fall. The species is a host plant for the Baltimore checkerspot butterfly and is pollinator-friendly.

care.short: Stake only if shade produces weak stems; avoid crowding and drying
care.guidance: NC State notes that too much shade may make staking necessary and that mildew can occur when soil becomes too dry or plants are overcrowded. Maintain the moist garden conditions described for the species; these observations do not establish container or hydroponic requirements.

problems.short: Mildew may follow dry soil or crowding; excessive shade can cause leaning
problems.guidance: NC State reports no significant problems overall, but notes mildew when soil is too dry or plants are crowded, and possible need for staking in excessive shade. Treat these as conditional signals, not inevitable disease or support needs.

name: Green Columbine
summary: A compact Asian perennial with nodding yellowish-green flowers. NC State describes a 1–3 ft plant with roughly 1 ft spread; its trait table gives a slightly broader height range, retained as a source-range caveat rather than a cultivar measurement.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies Green Columbine as Aquilegia viridiflora in Ranunculaceae and describes it as native to Asia. This profile is species-specific, not a generic account of Aquilegia hybrids.

growth.short: Compact, mounding perennial; green nodding flowers
growth.guidance: NC State describes a compact perennial with a basal mound of blue-green compound leaves and nodding yellowish-green flowers. Its narrative reports about 1–3 ft height and 1 ft spread; the trait table gives 8 in–3 ft height and 8 in–1 ft width. The source difference is retained rather than collapsed into a precise cultivar size.

cultivation.short: Moist, well-drained soil; full sun to dappled or partial shade
cultivation.guidance: NC State says the species grows in average-to-rich, moist, well-drained soil and is intolerant of heavy, poorly drained ground. It tolerates full sun through dappled/partial shade; light shade can prolong flowering. This is outdoor garden guidance, not hydroponic or grow-light advice.

flowering.short: Fragrant green flowers in late spring to early summer
flowering.guidance: NC State describes small, nodding yellowish-green flowers, generally in late spring to early summer. Light shade is reported to prolong the bloom season; no exact bloom date is universal across climates.

maintenance.short: Remove spent flowers for another flush; cut back declining foliage later
maintenance.guidance: NC State recommends removing flowers to encourage more blooms. It says blue-green foliage can remain attractive after flowering with regular irrigation, then be cut to ground level when it declines toward the end of summer. Timing is based on plant condition, not a fixed calendar.

propagation.short: Perennial that can self-seed; no germination protocol assigned here
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed as a propagation strategy and says Green Columbine can self-seed under favorable landscape conditions. The source does not establish sowing depth, temperature or a reliable germination schedule; those details are not invented.

problems.short: Occasional leafminer, aphid and columbine-borer issues
problems.guidance: NC State lists leafminers, aphids and columbine borer as infrequent insect problems and reports deer/rabbit resistance. Watch for those signs; resistance is not immunity. The page does not establish a cultivar-specific disease-resistance claim.

name: Flowering Tobacco Hybrid
summary: A seed-grown ornamental hybrid derived from Nicotiana alata and N. forgetiana. It must remain distinct from true N. alata; hybrid cultivars differ in fragrance and day/night bloom behavior.

identity.guidance: NC State identifies N. × sanderi as a hybrid of N. alata and N. forgetiana and distinguishes it from the species N. alata.

growth.short: Erect hybrid; UMass reports 18–36 in across varieties, not a cultivar guarantee
growth.guidance: NC State lists an erect habit and rapid growth. UMass Extension describes Flowering Tobacco as an upright annual and reports 18–36 inches across varieties. Because this identity specifies no cultivar, preserve that as a variety range rather than assigning one height or spread to every N. × sanderi selection.

cultivation.short: Full sun and average, well-drained soil; annual bedding/container use is documented
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes the hybrid as performing best in full sun and average, well-drained soil, with light shade tolerated. UMass Extension describes it as an annual for bedding and containers. NC State's summary table also lists an herbaceous-perennial plant type alongside its annual life-cycle field, so Garden treats annual use as the documented garden context and does not promise overwintering. Neither source establishes minimum pot dimensions or hydroponic suitability.

flowering.short: Green, pink or white tubular blooms in summer/fall; size and fragrance vary by cultivar
flowering.guidance: NC State describes green, pink or white tubular flowers, 1–3 inches across, with long corollas ending in a five-pointed star, and lists summer and fall bloom. UMass describes summer flowering. The named 'Sensation Mixed' is specifically fragrant and evening-flowering; those traits are not generalized to all N. × sanderi cultivars.

propagation.short: Seed propagation is documented; cultivar traits vary
propagation.guidance: NC State describes this hybrid as easy to propagate from seed. Its approximately 10-week statement concerns seed-to-flower timing, not an established-plant schedule or a guarantee for an unspecified cultivar. The source supplies no numeric germination protocol.

problems.short: All plant parts are poisonous
problems.guidance: NC State explicitly warns that all parts of this hybrid are poisonous. Keep away from children and pets; do not use as food.
